params.question: Breastfeeding reduces the risk of postpartum haemorrhage. Which mechanism best explains this benefit?

answers.text: Breast milk proteins stimulate platelet aggregation in the mother

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Breast milk proteins do not affect maternal platelet function. The reduction in postpartum haemorrhage is due to oxytocin-mediated uterine contraction during breastfeeding.

answers.text: Prolactin released during suckling contracts the uterine myometrium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Prolactin drives milk production by acting on alveolar cells. It does not cause uterine contraction. Oxytocin is the hormone responsible for myometrial contraction.

answers.text: Oxytocin released during suckling contracts the uterine myometrium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Suckling stimulates oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary. This oxytocin contracts uterine smooth muscle, promoting involution and reducing postpartum haemorrhage.

answers.text: Reduced blood volume from milk production lowers uterine blood flow

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Milk production does not significantly reduce maternal blood volume. The protective mechanism is oxytocin-mediated myometrial contraction, not a haemodynamic change.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key link is: suckling → oxytocin release → uterine contraction → reduced postpartum haemorrhage. This is a hormonal mechanism independent of the milk's nutritional content.
Well done. Oxytocin serves a dual role during breastfeeding — it triggers the milk ejection reflex in the breast and simultaneously contracts the uterine myometrium, reducing postpartum bleeding.

interactions.label: The 2018 BFHI revision groups its 10 steps into two areas: critical management p

params.question: The 2018 BFHI revision groups its 10 steps into two areas: critical management procedures and key clinical practices. Which of the following is classified as a key clinical practice?

answers.text: A written institutional breastfeeding policy communicated to all staff

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A written breastfeeding policy is a critical management procedure — it sets the institutional framework but is not a direct bedside clinical interaction with the mother-baby dyad.

answers.text: Mandatory staff competency training on lactation support

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Staff training is classified under critical management procedures. It builds workforce capacity but is not a direct clinical practice at the bedside.

answers.text: Rooming-in of mother and infant throughout day and night

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Rooming-in is a key clinical practice. It enables on-demand feeding, which drives the frequent prolactin surges needed to establish and maintain milk supply.

answers.text: Antenatal counselling on the benefits of breastfeeding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Antenatal education is grouped under critical management procedures in the 2018 BFHI revision, not key clinical practices.

overallFeedback.feedback: The 2018 BFHI distinguishes critical management procedures (policy, training, antenatal education) from key clinical practices (skin-to-skin, rooming-in, responsive feeding, avoiding supplements and pacifiers, community referral). Each clinical practice has a direct physiological rationale.
Well done. Key clinical practices include skin-to-skin contact, rooming-in, responsive feeding, avoiding unnecessary supplementation, avoiding pacifiers, and referral to community support.

interactions.label: A primiparous mother has persistent nipple pain during feeds on day 2. On observ

params.question: A primiparous mother has persistent nipple pain during feeds on day 2. On observation, the baby's mouth covers only the nipple, with equal areola visible above and below the lips. What is the single most important correction?

answers.text: Apply purified lanolin before each feed to reduce friction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Lanolin can soothe damaged nipples but does not address the root cause. Persistent pain through feeds almost always signals a latch problem — correcting the latch must come first.

answers.text: Switch to formula feeds until the nipples have healed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Stopping breastfeeding reduces the suckling stimulus, lowers prolactin, and may introduce nipple confusion. The priority is to correct the latch so breastfeeding can continue without trauma.

answers.text: Achieve a deeper, asymmetric latch with more areola visible above the upper lip than below

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. An asymmetric latch positions the lower jaw closer to the base of the nipple, allowing the tongue to compress the lactiferous sinuses effectively. This improves milk transfer and eliminates nipple trauma.

answers.text: Express milk manually and feed by cup until the soreness resolves

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cup feeding is a bridge strategy for preterm infants or temporary separation. Here, the priority is to correct the latch so the mother can continue direct breastfeeding without pain.

overallFeedback.feedback: The root cause of persistent nipple pain is almost always a shallow or symmetric latch. The fix is a deeper, asymmetric latch where more areola is visible above the upper lip than below — this positions the tongue correctly to compress the lactiferous sinuses.

Well done. The infant feeds from the nipple-areola complex, not the nipple alone. A deeper, asymmetric latch lets the tongue strip milk from the lactiferous sinuses in a peristaltic wave, preventing trauma and ensuring efficient milk transfer.

interactions.label: Infective and non-infective mastitis can be reliably distinguished on clinical e

params.question: Infective and non-infective mastitis can be reliably distinguished on clinical examination alone.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Actually, infective and non-infective mastitis present very similarly — both show localised redness, warmth, and tenderness. Neither examination nor the degree of redness reliably distinguishes them. That is why empirical antibiotics are given when the mother is febrile and systemically unwell — the risk of under-treatment outweighs a short antibiotic course.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. The clinical features of infective and non-infective mastitis overlap considerably. Because missing a bacterial infection risks abscess formation, most febrile, symptomatic cases are treated empirically with antibiotics.

interactions.label: A hospital administrator asks you to justify implementing the Baby-Friendly Hosp

params.question: A hospital administrator asks you to justify implementing the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative. Which argument best combines physiological and epidemiological evidence?

answers.text: The initiative requires minimal staff training and can be implemented at no additional cost

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is factually incorrect. BFHI requires substantive investment in staff training — it is one of the critical management procedures in the 2018 framework.

answers.text: Skin-to-skin contact maximises oxytocin release, and BFHI-designated hospitals show higher breastfeeding initiation and duration rates

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This combines physiological evidence (skin-to-skin triggers oxytocin release, supporting milk ejection and bonding) with epidemiological evidence (BFHI has been linked to higher breastfeeding initiation, exclusivity, and duration across countries at every income level).

answers.text: Formula feeding is associated with higher hospital costs due to procurement expenses alone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While formula has procurement costs, this argument ignores the far stronger physiological and health-outcome evidence for breastfeeding, which is the real justification for BFHI.

answers.text: Rooming-in primarily reduces nursing workload by shifting infant care to mothers

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rooming-in supports on-demand feeding and prolactin-driven milk production — its purpose is clinical, not labour-saving. Misrepresenting it as a cost-cutting measure undermines its physiological rationale.

overallFeedback.feedback: The strongest justification for BFHI integrates two lines of evidence: physiological (e.g., skin-to-skin maximises oxytocin release for milk ejection) and epidemiological (BFHI-designated hospitals show higher breastfeeding initiation, exclusivity, and duration across countries at every income level).

Well done. A strong BFHI justification links its clinical practices to lactation physiology (each step supports oxytocin or prolactin pathways) and to population-level evidence of improved breastfeeding outcomes.
